source.title: When Currencies Break
source.summary: Currency crises in Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Iran, and Lebanon. The dollar creates vulnerability, but governance determines the outcome.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Turkey's crisis was Erdogan overriding central bank independence. Pakistan's reflects institutional failure across the board. Egypt's is structural economic narrowness. Iran's combines sanctions with internal dysfunction. Lebanon's is elite capture of the entire banking system. Each case gets specific, fair treatment, with no heroes and no villains. The common thread: the dollar system creates vulnerability for peripheral economies, but domestic governance determines whether that vulnerability becomes a crisis. The same external pressures produce very different outcomes depending on how countries are governed.

x.single_post: Most people think currency crises happen because countries run out of dollars. They happen because leaders destroy the institutions that manage dollars. Turkey's Erdogan fired his central bank governor three times in two years.
thread: Five Muslim countries faced currency collapse in recent years. Each story reveals something different about how institutions break.
Turkey's crisis was political. Erdogan fired his central bank governor three times in two years, demanding lower rates while inflation soared.
Pakistan's reflects deeper rot. Every institution failed simultaneously. Egypt's economy is too narrow. Iran faces sanctions plus internal dysfunction.

Lebanon is different. The entire banking system was captured by elites who used deposits to fund government deficits. A Ponzi scheme disguised as sovereignty. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-mm-4

linkedin.post: Currency crises reveal more about governance than economics. Recent collapses in Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Iran, and Lebanon each tell a distinct story about institutional failure. Turkey's crisis was political interference: Erdogan fired his central bank governor three times in two years, demanding lower rates while inflation soared. Pakistan reflected systemic breakdown across all institutions. Egypt's narrow economic base couldn't withstand external pressures. Iran combines sanctions with internal dysfunction. But Lebanon stands apart: elites captured the entire banking system, using deposits to fund government deficits in what amounted to a Ponzi scheme. The dollar system creates vulnerability for peripheral economies, but domestic governance determines whether that vulnerability becomes catastrophe. Same pressures, different institutions, vastly different outcomes. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-mm-4
